games.title: Leishmania: quick quiz
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 2 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which insect vector is primarily responsible for transmitting Leishmania species in the Old World?
questions.explanation: Leishmania species in the Old World are transmitted to humans by the bite of infected female Phlebotomus sandflies.

questions.q: Which morphological stage of Leishmania is found intracellularly within human macrophages?
questions.explanation: The amastigote is the intracellular, non-flagellated form of Leishmania that multiplies within host macrophages.

questions.q: A patient presents with prolonged irregular fever, massive splenomegaly, weight loss, and pancytopenia. A bone marrow biopsy reveals intracellular organisms with a nucleus and kinetoplast inside macrophages. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar) classically presents with prolonged fever, massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, and intracellular amastigotes in bone marrow macrophages.

questions.q: Which Leishmania species is most characteristically associated with mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (espundia)?
questions.explanation: Leishmania braziliensis is the primary cause of mucocutaneous leishmaniasis, leading to destructive lesions of the nasopharyngeal mucosa.

questions.q: What stage of the Leishmania parasite is injected into the human host during a sandfly blood meal?
questions.explanation: Female sandflies inject the flagellated promastigote stage into the skin of the human host during a blood meal.

questions.q: Which biochemical abnormality is characteristically observed in patients with advanced visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Visceral leishmaniasis characteristically causes marked polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia along with pancytopenia.

questions.q: Post-Kala-azar Dermal Leishmaniasis (PKDL) is a cutaneous sequela that primarily occurs following infection with which organism?
questions.explanation: Post-Kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis is a cutaneous sequela that develops following visceral leishmaniasis caused by Leishmania donovani.

questions.q: Which of the following is an effective oral medication used in the treatment of visceral leishmaniasis?
questions.explanation: Miltefosine is the primary oral antiparasitic medication used to treat visceral leishmaniasis.

questions.q: Which diagnostic method is considered the definitive standard for confirming visceral leishmaniasis?
options: Stool microscopy for ova and parasites
Microscopic identification of amastigotes in tissue aspirates
Urine dipstick test for parasite antigens
questions.explanation: Visualization of amastigotes (Leishman-Donovan bodies) in splenic or bone marrow aspirate smears is the definitive diagnostic standard for visceral leishmaniasis.

questions.q: Which sandfly genus is responsible for the transmission of Leishmania in the Americas (New World)?
questions.explanation: In the New World (the Americas), Leishmania species are transmitted to hosts by sandflies of the genus Lutzomyia.

games.title: Physiological Changes of Pregnancy by System: quick quiz
games.topic: Physiological Changes of Pregnancy by System
games.blurb: Quiz for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which of the following cardiovascular changes typically occurs during the second trimester of a normal pregnancy?
options: Decrease in mean arterial blood pressure (MAP)
questions.explanation: Progesterone causes systemic smooth muscle relaxation, leading to a fall in systemic vascular resistance and a drop in blood pressure that reaches its lowest point in the second trimester.

questions.q: What is the primary mechanism responsible for physiological anemia observed during normal pregnancy?
options: Increased erythrocyte destruction in the maternal spleen
Greater expansion of plasma volume compared to red blood cell mass
Decreased maternal erythropoietin production in response to estrogen
Fetomaternal hemorrhage causing chronic blood loss
questions.explanation: Plasma volume increases by approximately 45-50% while red blood cell mass increases by only 20-30%, resulting in hemodilution.

questions.q: Which arterial blood gas finding is characteristic of a normal pregnant woman at term?
questions.explanation: Progesterone directly stimulates the central respiratory center to increase minute ventilation, creating a compensated respiratory alkalosis with a reduced PaCO2 and proportional decrease in serum bicarbonate.

questions.q: How do renal hemodynamics alter during normal pregnancy, and what is the expected effect on baseline serum creatinine levels?
options: GFR remains unchanged; serum creatinine decreases
questions.explanation: Renal blood flow and GFR increase by 40-50% during pregnancy, leading to increased solute clearance and lower normal serum creatinine levels.

questions.q: A 28-week pregnant woman has routine blood tests showing an isolated elevation of serum alkaline phosphatase (ALP) to twice the upper limit of normal for a non-pregnant adult. All other liver function tests are normal. What is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Perform an urgent abdominal ultrasound to evaluate for choledocholithiasis
Reassure the patient that this is a normal physiological finding
Start low-dose ursodeoxycholic acid for intrahepatic cholestasis
Perform a viral hepatitis serology panel
questions.explanation: Serum alkaline phosphatase increases substantially in normal pregnancy due to heat-stable ALP isoenzyme production by the placenta.

questions.q: Which pattern of thyroid function test results is expected during the first trimester of a normal pregnancy?
options: Decreased Total T4, increased TSH, normal Free T4
Increased Total T4, transiently decreased TSH, normal Free T4
Decreased Total T4, decreased TSH, decreased Free T4
Increased Total T4, markedly increased TSH, increased Free T4
questions.explanation: Estrogen increases hepatic synthesis of thyroid-binding globulin (raising total T4), while high early hCG levels weakly stimulate TSH receptors, causing a transient suppression of TSH while free T4 remains normal.

questions.q: Which lung volume parameter is significantly decreased during the third trimester of pregnancy due to diaphragmatic elevation?
questions.explanation: The expanding uterus elevates the diaphragm by approximately 4 cm, reducing the functional residual capacity by 10-20% near term.

questions.q: Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state. Which combination of blood changes contributes directly to this physiological adaptation?
options: Decrease in fibrinogen and decrease in Factor VIII
Increase in free Protein S and decrease in Factor V
Increase in fibrinogen and decrease in free Protein S
questions.explanation: Pregnancy increases hepatic synthesis of clotting factors (such as fibrinogen and Factor VIII) and decreases natural anticoagulants like free Protein S to reduce hemorrhage risk at delivery.

questions.q: Which hormone is primarily responsible for ligamentous laxity of the pelvic joints during pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Relaxin, secreted by the corpus luteum and placenta, causes collagen softening and relaxation of pelvic ligaments and the pubic symphysis.

questions.q: Which physical examination finding in the cardiovascular system is considered normal in a healthy pregnant woman at 32 weeks gestation?
options: New onset irregular heart rhythm with diffuse crackles
questions.explanation: A third heart sound (S3) and soft systolic ejection murmurs are common physiological findings due to hyperdynamic circulation and increased blood volume during late pregnancy.

games.title: Nephrotic Syndrome: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy presents with a 3-day history of periorbital edema, abdominal distension, and frothy urine. Urinalysis reveals 4+ proteinuria, and serum albumin is 18 g/L. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in young children, presenting with heavy proteinuria, severe hypoalbuminemia, and generalized edema.

questions.q: A 3-year-old girl with newly diagnosed, uncomplicated nephrotic syndrome presents to the pediatric clinic. Urinalysis demonstrates 4+ proteinuria, blood pressure is normal, and serum complement (C3/C4) levels are normal. What is the next best step in initial management?
questions.explanation: Empirical treatment with high-dose oral corticosteroids is the standard first-line management for typical idiopathic childhood nephrotic syndrome without requiring prior renal biopsy.

questions.q: A 5-year-old boy with steroid-responsive nephrotic syndrome presents to the emergency department with fever, severe abdominal pain, and diffuse abdominal tenderness. On examination, he has generalized edema, a temperature of 38.8°C, and abdominal guarding. What is the most likely complication?
questions.explanation: Children with active nephrotic syndrome are at increased risk for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, due to urinary loss of immunoglobulins and complement factors.

questions.q: A 2-month-old infant girl presents with severe generalized edema, failure to thrive, and heavy proteinuria present since birth. Placental weight was noted to be unusually large at delivery. Which gene mutation is most commonly associated with this condition?
questions.explanation: Congenital nephrotic syndrome of the Finnish type presents in the first three months of life with a characteristically large placenta and is caused by mutations in the NPHS1 gene encoding nephrin.

questions.q: An 8-year-old girl with nephrotic syndrome fails to enter remission after 4 weeks of standard daily high-dose prednisolone therapy. Urinalysis continues to show 4+ proteinuria with persistent generalized edema. What is the next best step in management?
options: Extend high-dose prednisolone for 4 more weeks without investigation
Discharge home on ACE inhibitors alone
questions.explanation: Steroid-resistant nephrotic syndrome, defined as persistent proteinuria despite 4 weeks of daily corticosteroid therapy, is a primary indication for a renal biopsy to investigate underlying histology such as focal segmental glomerulosclerosis.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy with active nephrotic syndrome develops sudden right flank pain and gross hematuria. Laboratory studies reveal a serum albumin of 15 g/L and an acute rise in serum creatinine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Nephrotic syndrome creates a hypercoagulable state through urinary loss of antithrombin III and increased synthesis of clotting factors, predisposing patients to renal vein thrombosis.

questions.q: A 4-year-old boy diagnosed with Minimal Change Disease is started on daily high-dose prednisolone therapy. His parents ask about routine childhood immunizations while he is on high-dose immunosuppressive treatment. Which vaccine is strictly contraindicated at this time?
questions.explanation: Live attenuated vaccines, such as MMR and varicella, are contraindicated during high-dose systemic corticosteroid treatment due to the risk of uncontrolled vaccine-induced infection.

questions.q: A 12-year-old boy presents with facial swelling, hypertension, and tea-colored urine. Laboratory workup reveals low serum C3 levels, raised anti-streptolysin O (ASO) titers, and microscopic hematuria with mild proteinuria. Which finding most strongly points away from Minimal Change Disease?
options: Low serum C3 and gross hematuria
questions.explanation: Minimal Change Disease typically manifests with normal serum complement levels and absent or microscopic hematuria, whereas low C3 and dark red/tea-colored urine strongly indicate nephritic syndrome such as post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.

games.title: Biliary tract disease: case showdown
games.blurb: Case Showdown for Year 4 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: A 42-year-old woman presents with severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain, fever, and nausea after eating a fatty meal. Physical examination reveals tenderness in the right upper quadrant with inspiratory arrest on deep palpation (Murphy sign). Ultrasound shows a thickened gallbladder wall (5 mm) and pericholecystic fluid. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The combination of right upper quadrant pain, fever, positive Murphy sign, and ultrasound evidence of gallbladder wall thickening and pericholecystic fluid confirms acute cholecystitis.

questions.q: A 68-year-old man presents with fever, jaundice, and right upper quadrant abdominal pain. On examination, he is confused and hypotensive with a blood pressure of 85/50 mmHg. Laboratory studies reveal severe leukocytosis and elevated direct bilirubin. What is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: The patient presents with Reynolds pentad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain, hypotension, and altered mental status) indicating severe acute cholangitis, which requires urgent biliary decompression via ERCP along with broad-spectrum antibiotics.

questions.q: A 34-year-old man with a history of ulcerative colitis presents with fatigue, pruritus, and mild jaundice. Laboratory testing shows a predominantly cholestatic pattern of elevated liver enzymes with an alkaline phosphatase level of 450 U/L. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) demonstrates multifocal strictures and segmental dilations of the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Primary sclerosing cholangitis is strongly associated with ulcerative colitis and characteristically displays a 'beaded' appearance of the biliary tree on MRCP.

questions.q: A 50-year-old woman presents with progressive fatigue and generalized itching for the past six months. On examination, she has xanthelasma and hepatomegaly, but no scleral icterus. Serum alkaline phosphatase is markedly elevated, and antimitochondrial antibodies (AMA) are positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Primary biliary cholangitis typically affects middle-aged women presenting with fatigue, pruritus, elevated alkaline phosphatase, and positive antimitochondrial antibodies.

questions.q: A 55-year-old woman presents with intermittent right upper quadrant pain radiating to the back, dark urine, and pale stools. Serum bilirubin is elevated at 5.2 mg/dL with marked elevation of alkaline phosphatase, while lipase is within normal limits. Ultrasound reveals a common bile duct diameter of 9 mm with a hyperechoic shadow in the distal duct without gallbladder wall thickening. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Obstructive jaundice accompanied by common bile duct dilation and a ductal stone on ultrasound without systemic inflammatory signs points to choledocholithiasis.

questions.q: A 38-year-old woman presents with recurrent episodes of postprandial right upper quadrant pain that last approximately 2 hours and resolve spontaneously. She is afebrile, and her liver function tests and inflammatory markers are entirely normal. Abdominal ultrasound shows multiple gallstones without gallbladder wall thickening or common bile duct dilation. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Transient postprandial RUQ pain caused by temporary obstruction of the cystic duct by a gallstone without inflammatory changes or lab abnormalities defines biliary colic.

questions.q: An 78-year-old woman presents with severe colicky abdominal pain, distension, and vomiting. An abdominal CT scan reveals dilated loops of small bowel, gas within the biliary tree (pneumobilia), and a calcified mass in the right iliac fossa. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Rigler's triad (small bowel obstruction, pneumobilia, and an ectopic gallstone) is diagnostic for gallstone ileus caused by a cholecystenteric fistula.

questions.q: A 65-year-old man presents with progressive, painless jaundice, a 6 kg weight loss, and dark urine. Physical examination reveals a non-tender, palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier sign). CT scan demonstrates intrahepatic biliary ductal dilation with a focal mass at the junction of the right and left hepatic ducts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Painless jaundice with intrahepatic biliary dilation and a tumor located at the confluence of the main hepatic ducts is characteristic of a Klatskin tumor (hilar cholangiocarcinoma).

games.title: The Heme and Liver: drug duel
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 2 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which agent is the specific antidote for paracetamol (acetaminophen) hepatotoxicity, acting primarily by replenishing hepatic glutathione stores?
questions.explanation: N-acetylcysteine acts as a precursor for glutathione synthesis, allowing the liver to detoxify the reactive metabolite N-acetyl-p-benzoquinone imine (NAPQI).

questions.q: A 22-year-old patient diagnosed with Wilson's disease is prescribed penicillamine. What is the primary mechanism of action of penicillamine in this condition?
options: Inhibition of copper absorption in the intestinal mucosa
Chelation of excess copper to facilitate urinary excretion
Inhibition of hepatic delta-aminolevulinic acid synthase
questions.explanation: Penicillamine is a chelating agent that binds excess systemic copper to form a stable, soluble complex excreted by the kidneys.

questions.q: Which medication is administered intravenously to suppress hepatic delta-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) synthase activity during an acute crisis of Acute Intermittent Porphyria?
questions.explanation: Hemin delivers exogenous heme to hepatic tissue, providing negative feedback inhibition on ALAS1 to stop the overproduction of toxic porphyrin precursors.

questions.q: Lactulose is commonly used to treat hepatic encephalopathy in patients with liver cirrhosis. What is its main mechanism of reducing serum ammonia concentrations?
options: Direct chemical binding of free serum ammonia in circulation
Bacterial degradation into colonic organic acids that convert ammonia to non-absorbable ammonium
Competitive inhibition of bacterial urease in the stomach
Up-regulation of hepatic urea cycle enzymes
questions.explanation: Colonic bacteria metabolize lactulose into organic acids, lowering intestinal pH and trapping diffuse ammonia as non-absorbable ammonium ions in stool.

questions.q: A patient with beta-thalassemia major undergoing chronic blood transfusions develops secondary hepatic iron overload. Which orally active iron chelator is indicated for this condition?
questions.explanation: Deferasirox is an orally bioavailable iron-chelating drug designed to treat chronic iron overload caused by frequent blood transfusions.

questions.q: Which medication lowers serum unconjugated bilirubin in patients with Crigler-Najjar syndrome type II by inducing hepatic UDP-glucuronosyltransferase (UGT1A1)?
questions.explanation: Phenobarbital acts as an inducer of hepatic microsomes, specifically increasing UGT1A1 activity to reduce unconjugated bilirubin in Crigler-Najjar type II.

questions.q: A patient with primary biliary cholangitis suffers from severe pruritus related to cholestasis. Which drug reduces pruritus by binding bile acids in the intestinal lumen?
questions.explanation: Cholestyramine is an anion-exchange resin that binds bile acids in the gut lumen, interrupting enterohepatic circulation and relieving cholestatic pruritus.

questions.q: Ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) can be used for the non-surgical dissolution of small, radiolucent gallstones. What is its primary mechanism of action?
options: Decreasing hepatic secretion of cholesterol into bile
Direct chelation of calcium salts in gallstones
Enzymatic cleavage of cholesterol ester bonds
questions.explanation: Ursodeoxycholic acid reduces cholesterol secretion into bile and decreases intestinal cholesterol absorption, promoting dissolution of cholesterol gallstones.

games.title: Basic Pharmacology - Study Guide — — Basic Pharmacology III: drug duel
games.topic: Basic Pharmacology - Study Guide — — Basic Pharmacology III
games.blurb: Drug Duel for Year 3 and above, written fresh today.

questions.q: Which mechanism of action correctly describes the inotropic effect of digoxin?
questions.explanation: Digoxin exerts its positive inotropic effect by inhibiting the sarcolemmal Na+/K+-ATPase pump, which indirectly leads to increased intracellular calcium concentrations in cardiomyocytes.

questions.q: A 45-year-old man treated with the high-potency typical antipsychotic haloperidol develops severe muscle rigidity, hyperthermia, autonomic instability, and altered mental status. Which adverse reaction is he experiencing?
questions.explanation: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome is a life-threatening adverse reaction associated with dopamine-blocking agents like haloperidol, characterized by muscle rigidity, hyperpyrexia, autonomic instability, and altered mental status.

questions.q: Gentamicin belongs to the aminoglycoside class of antibiotics. Which of the following is a characteristic dose-dependent toxicity associated with this drug?
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are well known for causing irreversible ototoxicity and potentially reversible nephrotoxicity.

questions.q: Which mechanism of action is responsible for the antimicrobial activity of metronidazole against anaerobic bacteria?
options: Inhibition of bacterial cell wall synthesis via transpeptidase binding
Binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit to inhibit protein synthesis
Inhibition of DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV
Formation of toxic reactive intermediate metabolites that damage bacterial DNA
questions.explanation: Metronidazole is reduced by intracellular electron transport proteins in anaerobic organisms to form toxic reactive intermediates that disrupt bacterial DNA.

questions.q: Propofol is a widely used intravenous general anesthetic agent. What is its primary mechanism of action?
options: Inhibition of central alpha-2 adrenergic receptors
questions.explanation: Propofol exerts its sedative and hypnotic effects primarily by acting as a positive allosteric modulator to enhance GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibitory neurotransmission.

questions.q: A patient with chronic gout is prescribed allopurinol for urate-lowering therapy. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
options: Inhibition of renal uric acid reabsorption
questions.explanation: Allopurinol lowers serum uric acid levels by inhibiting xanthine oxidase, the key enzyme responsible for converting hypoxanthine to xanthine and xanthine to uric acid.

questions.q: Ipratropium bromide is commonly prescribed in the management of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). What is its drug class and mechanism of action?
options: Leukotriene receptor antagonist reducing airway inflammation
questions.explanation: Ipratropium bromide is a short-acting muscarinic antagonist (SAMA) that produces bronchodilation by competitively blocking M3 acetylcholine receptors in bronchial smooth muscle.

questions.q: A 60-year-old male with heart failure is started on spironolactone. Which of the following is a potential side effect directly related to its mechanism as an aldosterone receptor antagonist?
questions.explanation: Spironolactone blocks aldosterone receptors in the late distal tubule and collecting duct of the kidney, inhibiting sodium reabsorption and potassium excretion, which can lead to hyperkalemia.
